say: Imagine your app gets this support message.
My payouts have been failing for three days.
Your code needs to decide two things.
Is this urgent?
And which team should get it?
A person knows the answer in one second.
But normal code can't read. It just sees a string of characters.

say: The first thing people try is keyword rules.
If the message says urgent, or ASAP, mark it high priority.
But look at our message.
It doesn't say either word, so the rule gets it wrong.
People never write the way your rules expect.
So you keep adding rules, and they keep missing.

slides.body:
Is this urgent? Which team?
This seems fairly urgent, as payout issues can affect cash flow. It might be best handled by billing, though it could also be a technical problem…

say: The second thing people try is asking a chatbot.
It understands the message just fine.
But it answers like this.
A whole paragraph. Seems fairly urgent. Probably billing. Could also be technical.
Now your code has to dig the answer out of that text.
And next time, the wording can be different, and your code breaks again.

say: This is the gap that Jev fills.
Jev is an AI model made by a company called TypeSafe.
It reads and understands language, like a chatbot does.
But it never writes you a paragraph.
It only answers with the options you gave it, plus a number that says how sure it is.
So you get the understanding of AI, with answers your code can use directly.

slides.label: What Jev is
slides.title: Why it's called System One
slides.body:
The name comes from the book Thinking, Fast and Slow.

System 1System 2
In peopleFast gut judgmentSlow, careful reasoning
In AIJevChat and reasoning models

⚡ One small judgment, in about 100 ms

Your code stays in charge. It asks Jev only when it needs common sense.
say: TypeSafe calls Jev a System One model.
The name comes from the book Thinking, Fast and Slow.
System one is your fast gut judgment. System two is slow, careful reasoning.
Jev is the fast kind.
It makes one small judgment, usually in about a tenth of a second.
It doesn't plan, and it doesn't take actions.
Your code stays in charge, and asks Jev only when it needs a bit of common sense.

slides.label: How it works
slides.title: You give it text and questions
slides.body:
📄 State“My payouts have been failing for 3 days.”
❓ Questionsas many as you need, three kinds
KindQuestionJev answers
noulDoes this convey urgency?0.95 chance of yes
choiceBilling, technical, or sales?billing
scoreCalm → frustrated → very angry1.4 on your scale
say: Here's how you use it.
You send Jev two things.
First, the state. That's the text you care about, here the customer's message.
Second, your questions. There are three kinds.
A noul is a yes or no question. You get back the chance of yes, like zero point nine five.
A choice picks one option from your list, like billing.
And a score places it on a scale you describe, like calm, frustrated, or very angry.
Jev answers all of them at the same time, in one request.

Jev is trained so these numbers match reality across many answers.

You pick the cut-offs by testing on your own data.
say: That number is the most useful part.
If Jev says zero point nine five, it's clearly urgent, so your code can page someone.
If it says zero point zero eight, it's clearly not.
But if it says zero point five five, Jev is unsure.
So your code can send that one to a person instead of guessing.
Jev is trained so that, across many answers, these numbers match what really happens.
You choose the cut-offs by testing on your own messages.

slides.label: The key rule
slides.title: Ask small questions
slides.body:
✗ Is this email spam?one answer hides many judgments
✓ Three small questionsDoes the sender match the company name?
Does it ask for a password?
Does it push you to act today?

Each small answer is easier to get right.

When a result looks wrong, you can see which part caused it.

Your code puts the answers together.
say: Here's the most important rule for getting good results.
Ask small, specific questions.
Don't ask, is this email spam? That hides many judgments in one answer.
Instead ask: does the sender match the company name? Does it ask for a password? Does it push you to act today?
Each small answer is easier to get right.
And when something goes wrong, you can see exactly which part caused it.
Then your own code puts the answers together.

say: Ready to try it?
Go to console.typesafe.ai, and create an API key.
Save it in your terminal as TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
Then send one request with the model, the state, and your questions.
The answer comes back under the same name you gave the question.
That's the whole API. One request in, one set of answers out.

slides.label: Try it
slides.title: Use the answer in your app
slides.body:
const jev = new TypeSafeClient();   // npm install @typesafe-ai/sdk
const { answers } = await jev.systemOne({
  state: { message },
  questions: {
    urgent: noul("Does this convey urgency?"),
    team: choice("Which team should handle this?",
      { billing: null, technical: null, sales: null }),
  },
});
if (answers.urgent.noul > 0.8) pageOnCall();
routeTo(answers.team.choice);
say: In a real app, you'll use the SDK.
Ask your questions, and get typed answers back.
Then it's just normal code.
If urgency is above zero point eight, page someone, and route the ticket to the team Jev picked.
Jev did the reading. Your code made the decision.

slides.label: Recap
slides.title: Jev in one sentence
slides.body:
Jev turns language into answers your code can use: your options, plus how sure it is.

  • It doesn't write text, chat, or take actions
  • It reads text only, and works best in English
  • Ask small questions, and let your code combine them
  • Use the number to decide when a person should check

Docs: docs.typesafe.ai
say: So, Jev in one sentence.
Jev turns language into answers your code can use: one of your options, plus how sure it is.
It doesn't write text, chat, or take actions.
It reads text only, and it works best in English.
Ask small questions, let your code combine them, and use the number to decide when a person should check.
That's Jev. The full docs are at docs.typesafe.ai.
